Hello! Welcome, glad to meet you today since this is your very first session together. Before we dive deep into the fishing incident you mentioned earlier, could we briefly outline what specifically brings you here and discuss how best to use our limited chair-time most productively for both of us? Please share whatever comes naturally to prioritize our path forward.

Hi, thanks for having me. Honestly, I'm here because I've been feeling really down about myself lately, all because of fishing. I used to love going out on weekends to relax, but now every time I go, I just end up feeling like a total failure. I guess I want to figure out why I can't stop thinking I'm the worst fisherman alive, and maybe get back to enjoying it again.

Thank you for sharing that openly; hearing that these trips shifted from relaxation sources to places of judgment helps ground our starting point. Can you walk me through the earliest moments yesterday evening when you realized you couldn’t shake the “worst fisherman” feeling, and roughly rate how distressed you felt compared to usual days? Understanding the precise timeline and intensity will help us pinpoint exactly where the negative cycle begins.

Well, yesterday evening I was just sitting on my couch, scrolling through my phone, and I saw a photo my friend posted of this huge bass he caught. Right away, that familiar sinking feeling hit me. I'd say the distress was probably a solid 7 out of 10, which is pretty standard for me lately whenever anything fishing-related comes up. It's like my whole mood just drops.

Noticing that specific visual—a large bass—and connecting it instantly to a sharp rise in discomfort tells me quite clearly that comparing your experience to others has triggered your core beliefs about failing. Can we trace that connection further? Did looking at his photo bring up memories of specific thoughts running through your head while you sat quietly waiting, perhaps wondering aloud *"If I hadn't woken up at midnight, surely they wouldn't have had luck either"*? Once we pin down that exact inner dialogue alongside the physical tension you described, we can examine how strongly it holds sway over your current outlook.

Yeah, it's like I immediately start running through everything I did wrong on my last trip. I remember thinking, "He probably knows some secret spot I'll never find," and "I bet he didn't even have to try that hard." Then my mind just spirals into all the times I came home empty-handed. My shoulders get all tight, and I just feel this heavy weight in my chest, like I'm worthless because I can't do something that seems so simple for everyone else.

Your description reveals a strong pattern where perceived laziness ("he didn't need to try") contrasts against your actual diligence, creating a harsh self-judgment that physically manifests as shoulder tightening and heaviness. Those thoughts seem to function less as observations and more as absolute truth judgments that erase your past successes and future hopes in a flash. Has noticing this sudden jump from "maybe he got lucky" to "**you** failed completely"** helped separate facts from stories your mind told itself afterward? Additionally, given that rating of seven-tenth distress, knowing that level of negativity drains enough motivation to avoid planning ahead—if avoiding outings prevents worsening outcomes—are we aiming primarily to reduce that acute heartache tomorrow or to build tools that prevent these visits from becoming emotionally damaging events once started?

I think I see what you're getting at... It's like my brain just skips over any possibility of luck or circumstances and goes straight to blaming me. I never really thought of it as a story my mind tells, it just feels like the truth. And honestly, I think I want both — I want to feel less awful in the moment when I see someone else's catch, but I also don't want the whole trip to be ruined before I even cast my line. Right now, just driving to the lake feels pointless because I already know I'm going to fail.

That’s a incredibly honest admission, and acknowledging that dual desire—to fix the pain AND save the activity—from wanting to reframe the meaning behind your frustrations. We’ve moved from identifying the problem (“it feels true”) to recognizing the cost (preventing engagement due to fear of failure)—a classic signpost in Cognitive Behavioral therapy known as **Avoidance**. By treating upcoming trips as certain failures beforehand, you’re protecting yourself from short-term agony but sacrificing long-term joy. 

To bridge these needs practically: 
Would you consider testing a modified rule for ourselves: *“On a planned outing, treat your primary objective as completing full prep/checklists successfully OR experiencing curiosity—not necessarily bringing home proof.”* Would framing the mission around presence and learning rather than production reduce the threat-level perception of impending doom? Or does maintaining strict realism (i.e., admitting odds vary wildly beyond your control) feel necessary until confidence rebuilds gradually? Either direction offers fertile ground for building sustainable balance soon.

I think the idea of focusing on the process instead of the outcome sounds... weird, but maybe it could help. Like, if I just go out there and tell myself I'm practicing or just observing, instead of needing to catch something to prove I'm not a failure. That feels a little less heavy, you know? But part of me still worries that even trying that, I'll just end up beating myself up anyway if I don't catch anything. I guess I'm scared to hope that changing my mindset will actually work.

That honesty is vital—and your caution speaks volumes about your integrity; however, history repeatedly proves that attempting harmful lies eventually collapses under scrutiny. Instead of abandoning certainty entirely, how about experimenting with a middle-ground stance: **"My effort determines my satisfaction, not the fish"**? Imagine placing bets on yourself where winning depends purely on executing your pre-planned routine flawlessly, leaving fate wholly untouched by variable elements like weather or water temperature.

Given this tentative framework, could outlining a simplified **“Perfect Effort”** checklist—which prioritizes logistics and behavior over results—serve as a safety valve should intrusive doubts return mid-trip? Specifically, would committing to tasks like parking safely, securing equipment properly, choosing varied locations strategically, and remaining engaged socially provide measurable anchors proving competence exists independently of catch numbers? Such structured repetition typically weakens rigid perfectionists over repeated exposure.

Hmm, that actually makes a lot of sense. If I could focus on stuff I can control, like making sure my gear is set up right or trying different spots instead of just giving up, then I'd have proof that I did my part. I think I could try making a little checklist like that before I go next time. Maybe if I check off "packed the right lures" and "tried three different casting techniques," I could feel like I actually accomplished something, even if the fish aren't biting. It's worth a shot, at least.

That pragmatic compromise strikes a real resonance because it replaces an uncertain fantasy with observable evidence of capability, effectively decoupling your self-worth from unpredictable nature conditions. To operationalize this quickly, would setting aside five minutes tonight to jot down that specific "Process Checklist" give you peace of mind tonight, ensuring you carry a reliable tool into the field this weekend? Plus, keeping it visible near your car seat serves as an impromptu reminder to refocus attention on controllable actions whenever the urge of comparison rises.

Yeah, I think I can do that. I'll write it out tonight before I go to bed, maybe even put it on my phone so I don't lose it. Having something concrete to look at when I start to spiral sounds like a good plan. Thanks, I actually feel a little bit lighter just thinking about having a plan instead of just dreading the whole thing.

That relief highlights exactly why behavioral experiments like this checklist work—they convert overwhelming uncertainty into manageable, step-by-step progress. Take care to send that note to your device tonight, and please reach out anytime if those "spiraled thoughts" ever sneak back unexpectedly; we can adjust the plan then. Until then, thank you for trusting me with this vulnerability.
Thanks, I really appreciate that. I'll make sure to get it done tonight. It helps knowing I can check in and adjust if things don't go as planned. I'll see how this weekend goes and let you know.

Please rest easy knowing that flexibility built into our protocol empowers you to course-correct easily if needed. Consider this a successful appointment because taking actionable responsibility for your mindset is half the battle fought. Drive safe, embrace the practice journey without attachment to immediate rewards, and welcome you warmly back anytime you seek clarification or support along the road ahead.

Hi. Thanks for asking. Honestly, this week has felt a bit heavier than before. I keep replaying that failed surgery in my mind, and it's making me dread going into the clinic. I think focusing on the main barrier today would help—I just can't seem to shake this feeling that I'm not good enough to be doing this job anymore.

It makes perfect sense that replaying the failure weighs heavily on you, especially because connecting that event to such a crushing belief—"you're simply incapable of holding onto your career"—shows exactly how deeply this pain affects every aspect of your identity. You mentioned wanting to focus on the *main* barrier keeping you stuck; looking closely, isn't that voice repeating "what happened at surgery = total loss of worth," effectively stopping all other possible paths ahead until its power fades? If we treat that specific equation—the link between one medical error and permanent professional inadequacy—as our target, have you noticed moments recently even slightly outside the hospital walls where your hands didn't tremble quite as badly, perhaps hinting that the worst-case scenario hasn't always manifested literally? Would exploring whether the intensity drops anywhere else give us leverage to chip away at that absolute certainty, or do we want to build a shield specifically designed to withstand the memory itself? Either direction honors your wish to confront the source, knowing fully well that dismantling the logic usually requires gathering smaller pieces of proof first.

I think I understand what you're saying... There have been a few quiet moments at home, like when I'm just petting our family dog or helping my kids with their homework, where I don't feel that heavy dread for a little while. But then I remember the surgery, and it all comes crashing back. I guess I haven't really noticed those breaks as proof of anything—I just see them as a temporary escape from the truth.

Noticing those quieter moments proves incredibly wise—you recognized instinctively that your ability to function wasn't entirely gone despite the catastrophic setback. By viewing those pauses merely as escapes rather than evidence of resilience, it seems you may be unintentionally dismissing powerful data points showing your competence persists alongside your struggle. Instead of waiting for days of flawless success to believe yourself worthy, what happens if we treated finding just one instance where you managed basic tasks successfully—even imperfect ones—as definitive proof that "failure at surgery doesn't erase who you are"? Can you recall one recent example where you handled responsibility reasonably well anyway, however fleeting that win seemed at the time? Identifying that exception often becomes the strongest foundation for rebuilding your self-trust piece by piece.

Well... there was one case yesterday. A little boy brought in his hamster with a swollen paw, and I managed to diagnose and treat it correctly. It wasn't a major surgery, just a minor infection, but the family was grateful and the hamster is doing better now. I didn't even think of that as anything positive until you asked—I just saw it as a simple case that anyone could have handled.

Hearkening recognition—that you initially overlooked your own victory—is a classic pattern known as minimization, where the brain filters successes to match expectations of failure. While treating the hamsters’ care as obvious common knowledge highlights your expertise, noting how easily it slipped beneath conscious notice reveals precisely how damaging that critical message ("only great surgeons succeed") must truly be for you to miss it unnoticed. Asking ourselves further: if acknowledging that incident required effort to surface afterward, shouldn't recognizing similar wins become automatic over time rather than relying solely on reminders? Might framing this task differently—from proving competence through isolation to accumulating tangible records of capable interactions—make reclaiming your professional pride feel less like defending a fortress and more like filling a portfolio of actual achievements? Shifting toward collecting objective examples rather than debating subjective intent changes the nature of the challenge significantly. Where does this line of thinking land you emotionally right this second?

It's... a bit of a relief, actually. I never thought to collect those small wins like evidence. I've just been focusing on the one big failure and using it to judge everything else. But if I really think about it, I have helped plenty of animals since then, even if they weren't difficult cases. Maybe I can start writing those down, just to remind myself.

Collecting those small victories shifts the entire dynamic from defensive justification to proactive documentation, giving you undeniable facts to counteract the distorted narrative that defined your experience post-surgery. Writing them down converts invisible hopes into verifiable reality, creating a personal archive that proves your skills remain intact regardless of isolated setbacks. To get started, imagine listing just **three** instances from the last month involving patients whose outcomes improved thanks to your care—not necessarily dramatic surgeries—but everyday problems solved competently. As you write them, consider labeling each entry with a specific detail that confirms your diagnostic reasoning or procedural execution worked flawlessly. Ready to draft this preliminary list, or shall we discuss potential pitfalls like forgetting entries mid-week? Your commitment to recording this evidence marks a significant stride toward separating your self-worth from singular events.

Okay, I can think of three right now. First, that hamster with the swollen paw from yesterday—I identified the infection quickly and prescribed the right antibiotics. Second, there was an elderly dog last week with arthritis; I adjusted its medication and the owner called two days later saying he was moving much better. Third, I successfully vaccinated a very anxious cat without sedation—it took patience, but the cat stayed calm and the owner was really relieved. Writing those down now, they don't feel small at all. They feel like real evidence.

Reflecting on those details already strengthens the argument immensely; describing the specific steps taken (identifying infections, adjusting meds, administering vaccines calmly) moves beyond mere optimism into observable competency that contradicts the "incompetent surgeon" lie. Notice how writing them out transformed your perception—they shifted from hidden memories to proud accomplishments, which naturally begins chipping away at the intense guilt surrounding the surgery. To close today, would you like to formalize this into a dedicated notebook section titled "Evidence Against Inadequate Performance," complete with space for weekly additions, ensuring you catch missed opportunities automatically? Confirming this final structural step gives us clarity on exactly how we proceed with this evidence-gathering mission.
